gbs333-aa3538-d1e107.summary: States the question: whether evident knowledge of theological truths is science properly so called.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e123.summary: Explains the question's occasion: since q. 1 showed that many purely theological truths can be evidently known by divine power, the question is whether such evident knowledge is science properly so called. For this reason some treat it not as a separate question but as an annex to q. 1.
claims: Many purely theological truths can be evidently known by divine power (from q. 1).
This question is sometimes treated as an annex to the first.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e148.summary: Outlines three articles: what a scientifically knowable proposition is; what science properly so called is; and, after notabilia and suppositions, the answer to the question.
claims: The question has three articles: the knowable proposition, science properly so called, and the answer.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e164.summary: First article: Ockham defines a proposition knowable by science properly so called as a necessary, doubtful proposition apt to be made evident by necessary propositions evidently applied to it through syllogistic discourse (cf. I d. 3 q. 4); briefly, a necessary, doubtful, and demonstrable proposition. The three conditions exclude respectively contingent propositions, self-evident propositions, and principles known by experience. Ockham raises and solves objections against this.
claims: A scientifically knowable proposition is necessary, doubtful, and demonstrable.
Contingent propositions, self-evident propositions, and experiential principles are excluded from being scibilia in the strict sense.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e197.summary: To understand the objections, distinguishes three senses of 'demonstration': most broadly, any syllogism from necessary premises; broadly, a syllogism from necessary premises prior to the conclusion, whether self-evident or doubtful (in these two senses even self-evident propositions are demonstrable); strictly and properly, a syllogism that produces knowing, whose necessary premises are apt to cause adhesive knowledge of the conclusion.
claims: 'Demonstration' is taken in three senses: any syllogism from necessary premises; such a syllogism from prior premises; a syllogism generating scientific knowledge.
In the first two senses self-evident propositions are demonstrable.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e226.summary: Second notandum: demonstrable propositions are of two kinds, resolvable into self-evident principles or into principles known by experience (a conclusion is 'resolved' into principles when proved by them). A self-evident proposition is not the same as an immediate, i.e., indemonstrable, one: many first immediate principles are known not per se but by experience, as Augustine's authority supports.
claims: Demonstrable propositions resolve either into self-evident principles or into experiential principles.
Self-evident and immediate are not the same: many immediate principles are known by experience, not per se.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e261.summary: Second article: science properly so called is evident knowledge of a necessary truth apt to be caused by premises applied to it through syllogistic discourse.
claims: Science properly so called is evident knowledge of a necessary truth apt to be caused by premises through syllogistic reasoning.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e274.summary: Notes that science could be defined more briefly in correspondence with the knowable proposition, and begins Ockham's clarifications of the definition's clauses. First: knowledge of a conclusion acquired by demonstration and by experience is of the same species, since they intensify each other, and degrees of different species cannot unite in one intensification (cf. d. 17).
claims: Knowledge of a conclusion acquired by demonstration and by experience are of the same species.
Only degrees of the same species can combine in intensification.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e304.summary: Second: knowledge of some principles and conclusions is had both by experience and by demonstration, while some conclusions are known only by demonstration; an example is the relation of sense and intellect, which agree in some respects and differ in others.
claims: Some truths are knowable both by experience and by demonstration; some only by demonstration.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e324.summary: Third: science of a necessary truth can be caused from a contingent truth, not demonstratively but experientially. A necessary truth cannot be demonstrated through a contingent premise, but from evident knowledge of one contingent and one necessary truth, not arranged in mode and figure, evident knowledge of a demonstrable conclusion can arise, as 'this herb heals, so every herb of this species heals'. The inference holds not by an intrinsic middle but by an extrinsic one: 'all agents of the same most specific species produce effects of the same kind, other things equal'. Sometimes one experience suffices for a principle of art or science, when the subject is a most specific species ('every heat heats'); sometimes many are needed, when the subject is common ('every act generates a habit' requires experience of each species of act). This holds when the principle is acquired solely by experience, not when it can be acquired by reasoning.
claims: Science of a necessary truth can be caused experientially from a contingent truth.
A necessary truth cannot be demonstrated from a contingent premise.
Inductive inference holds by an extrinsic middle: same-species agents produce effects of the same kind.
For a most specific species one experience can suffice; for a common term, experience of each contained species is required.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e415.summary: Fourth: science quia and science propter quid are each taken in two ways, which is plain enough.
claims: Science quia and propter quid each admit two senses.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e422.summary: Fifth: Ockham takes science properly so called not as distinguished from art or prudence but more generally, covering speculative and practical habits; it is distinguished from understanding (habit of principles) and wisdom (which for him is understanding and science together, the habit of a whole demonstration).
claims: Science properly so called here includes both speculative and practical habits.
Science is distinguished from understanding (of principles) and wisdom (of the whole demonstration).

gbs333-aa3538-d1e444.summary: Introduces the third article with general notabilia and suppositions to clarify this and later questions, to be proved in their proper places.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e457.summary: First supposition: science here means adhesive knowledge, actual or habitual, acquired or acquirable by demonstration.
claims: Science is adhesive knowledge acquired or acquirable by demonstration, actual or habitual.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e471.summary: Second supposition: a demonstration is a syllogism from necessary premises apt to generate evident knowledge of the conclusion.
claims: A demonstration is a syllogism from necessary premises apt to generate evident knowledge of the conclusion.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e480.summary: Corollary: in every demonstration the premises are better known than the conclusion, otherwise they could not generate its evident knowledge.
claims: In every demonstration the premises are better known than the conclusion.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e491.summary: A conclusion is demonstrable when it is not immediate, i.e., when there is a term to which the predicate belongs prior (more evidently) than to the conclusion's subject, which can serve as middle. Examples: 'man is capable of learning' through the intellective soul, to which that predicate belongs first; heat mediating between heating and 'heat-producing' (taken for a subject having heat). Recalls the definition of first subject from Prologue q. 3 (actually q. 4).
claims: A conclusion is demonstrable if and only if it is mediate, having a term to which the predicate belongs more evidently.
The intellective soul is the middle for demonstrating that man is capable of learning.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e537.summary: Third supposition, on distinctions in God (to be shown in d. 2 and elsewhere): in God there is really only the essence, the relations, the persons constituted from essence and relation, and what is constituted from essence and active spiration, all identical with the essence. Nothing in God is essentially distinct. Opposed relations are really distinct from each other but not from the essence, so the persons they constitute are really distinct. Relations and the constituted persons are formally distinct from the essence, and relations from the persons they constitute. Disparate relations (paternity and active spiration; filiation and active spiration) are only formally distinct. A relation is really distinct from the person constituted by the opposed relation (paternity from the Son). Beyond these there is no distinction in God: attributes such as goodness, wisdom, power, intellect, will, and love are distinct neither really, nor ex natura rei, nor formally, nor even by reason, since everything in God is a thing, and a thing is not distinguished by reason from a thing.
claims: In God there is nothing besides the essence, relations, and persons, all identical with the essence.
Opposed relations and the persons they constitute are really distinct from one another but not from the essence.
Relations and persons are formally distinct from the essence; disparate relations are only formally distinct.
Divine attributes such as wisdom, goodness, and power are not distinguished in any way, not even by reason.
There is no distinction of reason in God, since everything in God is a res.
concepts: rejection of distinctio rationis in God

gbs333-aa3538-d1e631.summary: Fourth supposition: concepts representing God are distinct or indistinct. A distinct concept represents its object in itself, with nothing else terminating the act through the concept or any part of it; such are intuitive cognitions or abstractive ones presupposing intuition. An indistinct concept is not of the thing in itself and represents, wholly or in part, something other than it. A concept of a thing in itself is one formed because the thing, present as object, moves the intellect. Naturally speaking, we can have distinct knowledge in this life of nothing not sensed, except certain of our own acts and passions, so a distinct cognition of God is naturally impossible for us in via.
claims: Concepts of God are either distinct (of God in himself) or indistinct.
Distinct concepts are intuitive or abstractive cognitions presupposing intuition.
Naturally, in this life we have distinct knowledge only of sensed things and some of our own inner acts.
Distinct cognition of God is naturally impossible for us in this life.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e679.summary: Divides indistinct concepts of God into common (to God and creatures) and proper (to God alone). Common concepts are absolute (being, substance, spirit, wisdom, justice, intellect, will, taken without connoting anything else) or connotative, and the connotative are affirmative (productive, conserving, destructive) or negative (immortal, incorporeal, indivisible).
claims: Indistinct concepts of God are common to God and creatures or proper to God.
Common concepts are absolute or connotative; connotative ones are affirmative or negative.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e711.summary: Proper concepts are absolute or connotative. Proper absolute concepts are simple or complex: simple ones cannot be had in via, but complex ones can (built from absolute terms such as substance, essence, justice, wisdom).
claims: Simple absolute proper concepts of God cannot be had in this life.
Complex absolute proper concepts of God can be had in this life.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e727.summary: Proper connotative concepts can be simple, such as 'creative', 'annihilative', 'infinite', 'eternal'; there are also complex proper connotative concepts.
claims: Simple connotative concepts such as 'creative' or 'infinite' are proper to God.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e736.summary: Fifth supposition, on the order of these concepts with respect to knownness: distinct concepts are prior, i.e., better known with respect to any predicate, than indistinct ones; every true proposition whose subject or predicate is a distinct concept of God is better known than any proposition formed from indistinct concepts.
claims: Distinct concepts of God are better known with respect to any predicate than indistinct ones.
Propositions involving distinct concepts of God are better known than those formed from indistinct concepts.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e767.summary: There is also an order among distinct concepts regarding their predicates: a predicate said formally of God belongs more evidently to a distinct concept than one said of God only by identical predication, such as personal and notional predicates. Also 'person' or 'suppositum' belongs to the Father or Son before the essence, and 'to create' belongs to the essence before the person, since it belongs to the persons by reason of the essence.
claims: Formal predicates of God are known prior to predicates holding only by identity, like notional ones.
'Person' belongs prior to Father or Son than to the essence.
'To create' belongs prior to the essence than to the persons.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e793.summary: Among indistinct concepts too there is an order: more common absolute concepts seem prior to less common ones with respect to other predicates, and convertible concepts prior to non-convertible ones.
claims: More common absolute concepts are prior to less common ones; convertible concepts are prior to non-convertible ones.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e809.summary: Responsive conclusion: every necessary, doubtful proposition affirming or denying something of God, whose predicate belongs to or is removed from some other term prior to the subject, is demonstrable, and only such is; evident knowledge of it is science properly so called. In short, every necessary, doubtful, mediate proposition about God is demonstrable.
claims: Every necessary, doubtful, mediate proposition about God is demonstrable.
Evident knowledge of such propositions is science properly so called.
Only such propositions about God are demonstrable.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e836.summary: First corollary: no necessary proposition both of whose extremes are distinct cognitions of God is demonstrable, since it is self-evident.
claims: Necessary propositions whose terms are both distinct concepts of God are self-evident and thus indemonstrable.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e845.summary: Second corollary: no necessary proposition one of whose extremes is a distinct cognition of God is demonstrable, since it is self-evident.
claims: Necessary propositions with even one extreme a distinct concept of God are self-evident and indemonstrable.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e856.summary: Third corollary: of propositions formed from indistinct cognitions of God, some (the necessary and mediate) are demonstrable, and others (the contingent or immediate) are not.
claims: Propositions about God formed from indistinct concepts are demonstrable if necessary and mediate, not if contingent or immediate.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e869.summary: Notes that the theory of this matter is sufficiently gathered from Ockham's conclusions, which, though numerous, are adequately captured in those given.

gbs333-aa3538-d1e878.summary: Concludes that Scotus's opinion, recited and attacked by Ockham, fails in two ways. First, there is no such order among essential attributes, notional attributes, and relations ad extra as Scotus imagines, and his principle does not hold. Second, even granting an order of rationes in God making one proposition prior to another, one would not be demonstrable through another, both because such priority does not suffice for demonstration and because all propositions formed from distinct concepts of God are self-evident and thus indemonstrable.
claims: Scotus's ordering of divine attributes (essential, notional, relational ad extra) does not exist.
Even such an order would not make one proposition about God demonstrable through another.
Propositions formed from distinct concepts of God are self-evident and indemonstrable.

gbs333-aa3538.summary: Quaestio 2 asks whether evident knowledge of theological truths, shown possible by divine power in q. 1, is science properly so called. Article 1 defines the scientifically knowable proposition as necessary, doubtful, and demonstrable, distinguishes three senses of demonstration, and separates self-evident from immediate principles, since many immediate principles are known by experience. Article 2 defines science as evident knowledge of a necessary truth apt to be caused by premises through syllogism. Clarifications follow: demonstrative and experiential knowledge of a conclusion are of one species; induction yields knowledge of necessary truths from contingent ones by an extrinsic uniformity principle; and science here covers practical and speculative habits and differs from understanding and wisdom. Article 3 adds suppositions. On the divine distinctions, only the persons and opposed relations are really distinct, relations are formally distinct from the essence, and attributes are distinct in no way, not even by reason. Concepts of God are distinct (of God in himself, naturally impossible in via) or indistinct, common or proper, absolute or connotative, and are ordered by knownness. The responsive conclusion is that every necessary, doubtful, mediate proposition about God is demonstrable, and its evident knowledge is science properly so called. Propositions with distinct concepts of God are self-evident and indemonstrable, while those from indistinct concepts are demonstrable if necessary and mediate. Scotus's ordering of divine rationes is rejected, as is the claim that it would ground demonstration.
claims: A scientifically knowable proposition is necessary, doubtful, and demonstrable; science is evident knowledge of such a truth caused by syllogistic discourse.
Necessary truths can be known evidently by experience through induction resting on an extrinsic uniformity principle.
In God only the persons (via opposed relations) are really distinct; attributes are not distinct even by reason.
In this life we have only indistinct concepts of God; a distinct concept is naturally impossible.
Every necessary, doubtful, mediate proposition about God is demonstrable, and evident knowledge of it is science properly so called; propositions involving distinct concepts of God are self-evident.
Scotus's order among divine rationes neither exists nor would ground demonstration.
concepts: distinct vs. indistinct concepts of God
